newsitem.title: ALBANIA: SOUTH ALBANIA REVELS IN LIKELY LEFTIST VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH ALBANIA REVELS IN LIKELY LEFTIST VICTORY.

text.p: Albania's Socialist party took a strong lead in early election results in this southern rebel town on Sunday, sending its jubilant armed supporters into a frenzy of celebratory shooting.

The sound of explosions reverberated across the harbour of the Adriatic port town, which has been at the mercy of armed gangs for four months, and youths fired everything from pistols to anti-tank missiles into the air.

With 25 percent of ballots counted, the Socialists had 55.5 percent of the vote against the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha, which had so far gained only 7.9 percent, Sarande's central electoral committee told reporters.
The Human Rights Party, which represents the large ethnic Greek minority in the south won 13.2 and the rest of the vote went to smaller parties and independent candidates.

Southern Albanians determined to oust Berisha in early elections voted in relative calm but with news of the first results, Socialist supporters raced through the town in cars draped with party flags, honking their horns and firing Kalashnikov rifles into the air.

The armed youths who usually roam the town had kept out of sight while a multinational force sent to guard Western election monitors was stationed in town. The soldiers left for their base in the town of Gjirokaster at dusk.

Southern Albania was the starting point for the upheaval sparked by the failure of five fraudulent investment schemes. More than 1,500 people have died in the mayhem. Southerners say Berisha is to blame for allowing the schemes to flourish.
"Nobody wants Berisha here. He ruined a lot of people and he's not democratic," said Kosta Koco, an engineer who was waiting in line with his family to cast his vote.
"We don't mind his party but the man himself, and nobody will vote for them."

The distant rattle of machine gun fire mingled with the music of clarinet and tambourine bands outside polling centres. The bands became a traditional feature during the single-party elections of the hardline communist regime that ruled Albania for 45 years until 1990.
In nearby villages dominated by the Greek minority, voters turned out in large numbers at polling stations after the tolling of church bells signalled the end of the Sunday Orthodox service.
Polls closed on time at 6 p.m. in most places, but one Sarande polling station remained open past the deadline to enable a crowd of latecomers to cast their votes.
Results trickled in from nearby villages, with local officials escorted by armed youths bringing the ballots stuffed in plastic bags to Sarande's municipal building for the count.

The depth of anti-Berisha feeling was demonstrated by a result officially declared within minutes at an old people's home in Gjirokaster, 40 km (25 miles) north of Sarande. Twenty-seven of 28 residents voted for the Socialist Party.

Observers said communications with remote villages were posing a problem but Sarande election officials said they were getting a steady flow of ballots from the countryside and expected to be counting them until early on Monday morning.
